gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit_Branch.cpp:30-41 emits native sc with flush+EXCEPTION_SYSCALL raise

gaps.name: Downcount subtraction (1-cycle vs variable-cycle ops)
gaps.why: Jit64 tracks variable cycle costs (div=36, mul=4, lmw=variable, etc.) and subtracts them from downcount on block exit. WASM uses 1-cycle-per-instruction (JitWasm.cpp:205), causing downcount to drain too slowly. Boot code often runs tight countdown loops or uses CoreTiming-driven state transitions (e.g., waiting for DVD DMA completion via downcount=0 interrupt). Slow downcount drain causes events to fire LATE, potentially missing deadline windows for state initialization or I/O synchronization. MP4 physics/PSO network code is sensitive to timing accuracy.
gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit.cpp:1003,587 uses js.downcountAmount = sum(opinfo->num_cycles); we use 1-cycle-per-instruction

gaps.name: fcmpu / fcmpo
gaps.why: Floating-point compare (fcmpu/fcmpo, opcode 63 sub10=0/32) updates CR field and may raise VX exception on SNaNs. Currently routes to WIMPORT_INTERP fallback. Boot code (especially OSContext FPU init) uses fcmpu to test NaN values and gate code paths. If the compare result is wrong (wrong CR bits set), subsequent conditional branches that depend on fcmpu results will mispredict, corrupting register initialization or jumping into wrong code path.
gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit_FloatingPoint.cpp:1089-1097 emits fcmpu/fcmpo with CR field + FPRF updates

gaps.name: Feature flag state tracking (IR/DR status at BLR)
gaps.why: Jit64 encodes MSR feature_flags (IR/DR virtual memory enable bits) in high-order bits of branch return address so WriteBLRExit can verify the bits match compile-time assumptions. If a BLR-following block is compiled with IR/DR=0 but executed with IR/DR=1, memory accesses use wrong virtual address mapping, causing reads/writes to wrong memory locations. Early boot toggles virtual memory on at kernel-entry; code compiled before toggle will produce garbage when executed after toggle.
gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit.cpp:582-584 encodes m_ppc_state.feature_flags in return-address high bits

gaps.name: GQR constant speculation gate
gaps.why: Paired-singles quantization (ps_* arithmetic ops) depend on GQR registers (graphics quantization registers, SPR 912-919). Jit64 verifies at block-entry that GQR values match compile-time expectations; if they diverge, it triggers a compile exception and re-compiles. Our WASM JIT lacks this gate. If a block's GQR values change mid-block (rare but possible in tight loops modifying GQRs), we silently use stale GQR values, causing quantization errors in subsequent ps_* ops. MP4/PSO use paired-singles heavily for matrix math; wrong quantization corrupts transformations.
gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit.cpp:975-983 emits CMP_or_TEST of GQR(gqr) against expected constant + jump to farcode on mismatch

gaps.name: fctiwx / fctiwzx
gaps.why: Float-to-integer conversion (fctiwx uses FPSCR rounding mode, fctiwzx truncates) are used in boot code to convert floats to signed integers for address/count calculations. Currently routes to WIMPORT_INTERP fallback. Fallback is semantically correct. However, if rounding mode is wrong or FPSCR is stale, truncation can produce off-by-one errors in loop counts or address offsets, causing loops to terminate early or crash.
gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit_FloatingPoint.cpp:1098-1139 emits fctiwx/fctiwzx with mode selection

gaps.name: mcrf / CR bit field operations
gaps.why: mcrf (move CR field) and crand/crandc/creqv/crnand (CR logical ops) are used in boot code to set up condition-register state before conditional branches. Missing dispatch (ppc_emit.cpp case 19 sub10 0,129,257,225,289) routes to WIMPORT_INTERP. If a block constructs CR bits via mcrf then immediately branches on them in the same block, the CR cache will be stale between ops (since fallback flushes), causing branch misprediction.
gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit.cpp dispatch_ops covers all opcode 19 variants via lXXx / crXXX tables

gaps.name: Gather pipe exception check
gaps.why: Jit64 emits a per-op TEST(EXCEPTION_EXTERNAL_INT) after each gather-pipe write and branches to far-code handler if CP/PE interrupt is pending and MSR.EE enabled. Our code only drains at block exit (ppc_emit.cpp:91-100). Missing mid-block checks mean CP-triggered GPU fences may not fire timely, delaying I/O completion. For boot sequences, this just increases latency; games haven't started yet so no real-time constraint violations occur.
gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit.cpp:1034-1062 wraps gather-pipe writes with EXCEPTION_EXTERNAL_INT check

gaps.name: Breakpoint dispatch (debugging)
gaps.why: Jit64 emits breakpoint checks at compile-time if FL_BREAKPOINT flag is set. Our code skips this entirely. Impact: breakpoints set on JIT-compiled instructions won't fire until cache eviction forces re-interpretation. Early boot doesn't use debugging, so this is only a dev-mode issue.
gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit.cpp:1084-1100 checks opinfo->flags & FL_BREAKPOINT and emits CheckAndHandleBreakPointsFromJIT

gaps.name: Speculative constant initialization
gaps.why: Jit64 analyzes block inputs and seeds MMIO/gather-pipe constants at block start, inserting verification checks. Our code has minimal constant-prop (only for MMIO address routing, jit_load_store.cpp:348-465). Missing speculative constants means blocks reuse stale constant assumptions, forcing slower addr-computation paths. For boot code with fixed MMIO addresses, the performance hit is measurable but doesn't affect correctness.

gaps.name: Register cache pre-load hints
gaps.why: Jit64 pre-binds multi-use inputs via PreloadRegisters to avoid redundant reloads between ops. Our RegCache binds on-demand, causing extra memory traffic for registers used multiple times per block. For boot code, this is just a few extra loads; negligible on the scale of early-game initialization.

gaps.name: Profiling prologue (performance monitoring)
gaps.why: Jit64 emits BeginProfiling calls at block entry when IsProfilingEnabled(). Our code skips this entirely. Impact: profiling infrastructure won't collect block timing data. Games don't use profiling in production, so this only affects developer telemetry.
gaps.reference: Jit64 Jit.cpp:936-937 emits BeginProfiling call at block start

gaps.name: ISI exception on address translation failure
gaps.why: Jit64 flags code_block.m_memory_exception after Analyze() if instruction fetch fails; our analyzer never sets this flag (ppc_analyst.cpp:250). Impact: if an instruction address cannot be translated, we emit it anyway. At runtime, mem.Read_U32(pc) has no ISI fallback path. Instruction-fetch failures are extremely rare (only happen with unmapped segments during exception handling); games boot normally.

gaps.name: lfsux / lfdux / stfsux (FP indexed loads with update)
gaps.why: FP indexed loads with RA update (lfsux/lfdux/stfsux, opcode 31 sub10 567/631/695) are used in OSContext save/restore. Currently route to WIMPORT_INTERP fallback, which is semantically correct (full flush/reload protocol at ppc_emit.cpp:70-106). Missing native emit just costs cycles during boot; no functional impact.

gaps.name: lfdx (FP double indexed load)
gaps.why: lfdx (opcode 31 sub10=599) is FP double load with indexed addressing, used in OSContext. Routes to WIMPORT_INTERP with full protocol. Semantically correct; missing native emit costs cycles only.

gaps.name: fselx (FP conditional select)
gaps.why: fselx (opcode 63 sub10=167) conditionally copies FD from FA or FC based on FA sign. Rare in boot code. Routes to WIMPORT_INTERP, which is correct. No functional impact on early boot.

gaps.name: Instruction skip tracking (merged op optimization)
gaps.why: Jit64 sets op.skip when certain ops can be merged (dcbt+dcbst sequences); the emitter skips them. Our code always processes every instruction, adding harmless dead code. Early boot is not sensitive to code size; no functional impact.

gaps.name: Block linking/unlinking (x86 patch infrastructure)
gaps.why: Jit64 patches block-to-block jumps at runtime via LinkBlock/UnlinkBlock infrastructure. WASM modules are immutable; every block exit writes PC and returns to dispatcher. Every dispatch is a hash-table lookup + conditional re-compile. Impact: slightly slower dispatch (lookup cost ~100ns, re-compile cost ~1ms if cache miss). Early boot tolerates higher dispatch overhead; games haven't started yet.
